newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand see rates flexibility after baht float.
newsitem.headline: Thailand see rates flexibility after baht float.

text.p: Thailand's central bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond said that the floating of the baht on Wednesday had given the central bank room for more interest rate flexibility and would spark more capital inflows.

"The new currency system will allow the Bank of Thailand more room to manage interest rates and will attract more inflows," he told the nation in a televised address. "Now we can have interest rates come down without having to defend the baht."
"In the past, not only did inflows decrease, there were also a lot of outflows causing liquidity problems," he said.
Rerngchai added that the movement of the baht on Wednesday after the flotation was announced early on Wednesday had been satisfactory.

After Thailand said it had switched to a managed float system for the baht from a peg to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar, the baht sank to a record low of around 29.00 to the dollar. However, it later stabilised to around 28.80 late on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya who also appeared on the telecast said the switch in the baht system had been made because the old system was unsuitable for the economy.
Thailand is going through its worst economic slump in over a decade with troubles in its finance and property sectors due to non-performing loans and poor asset quality.
"The basket of currencies system used to be suitable for the Thai economy because in the past 10 years the dollar was weak. Consequently this kept the baht weak," said Thanong.

"But in the past year, the situation has changed and the baht has strengthened against the yen and the mark, pushing it up when the economy slowed down, affecting our exports and capital inflows," he added.
Rerngchai said Thailand's exchange rate system had been a weak point for the country.

Since 1995 when the country faced economic instability, the authorities had tried to use both fiscal and monetary policies to solve them but they had not been effective because of the baht system making a stable unit and an easy prey for speculative attacks.
"That's why we decided to change the system," he said.

Thailand chose to float the baht at this time to switch currency systems because it was just after half-year book closing for Thai businesses and changes now would not complicate matters much for them.
